label: Lineage
heading: In conversation with
intro: Works the artist reads as kin — where the picture surface is treated as skin, and the mark as an incision. Shown here as links to the holding museums.

cards.title: Wounds
cards.text: A series of paper-pulp prints where the sheet is bruised and torn from within — the wound not depicted but pressed into the surface itself.

cards.title: Spatial Concept
cards.text: The canvas slashed and punctured — the cut as the work, the surface opened rather than painted upon.

cards.title: The Snail
cards.text: A spiral built from torn blocks of colour — sensation abstracted to its coil, a quiet companion to the cone-snail thread of the workshops.

essay_label: Drawing as a line of inquiry
essay:
The workshops at the NCBS Archives rest on an older claim: that drawing was one of the first instruments of natural science. In Rome in 1603 the Accademia dei Lincei — the Academy of the Lynxes, named for its all-seeing eye — set out to look at the world closely and record it. Its Paper Museum, assembled by Cassiano dal Pozzo, ran to thousands of drawings of natural and man-made things, and is credited with helping establish the ground rules of empirical science. Dal Pozzo's instruction still describes the method of these workshops: look at everything, but understand that insight often comes from attending to one thing, and drawing it again and again until you reach its essence. Francesco Stelluti's microscopic drawings of a bee, made for the Academy in 1630, are what that discipline produced when a lens was added to the eye.

Shells carry the same double life. An eleventh- or twelfth-century conch from eastern India or Bangladesh, carved with Lakshmi-Narayana, holds the shell as a sacred object. A century of Dutch and French still lifes — Jacques Linard's shells and coral of around 1640, Adriaen Coorte's of 1698 — holds it as a specimen, a curiosity and a proof: for Rumphius and his contemporaries, classification; for many of their patrons, natural theology, nature admired as evidence of divine making. That appetite had a name, conchylomania. K.S. Krishnan's cone shells in the NCBS Archives, collected for the analgesic peptides in their venom, sit at the end of that line — and Matisse's *Snail*, a spiral built from torn colour, sits alongside it.
note: Also read alongside: Santiago Ramón y Cajal's neuroanatomical drawings, Nalini Malani, Marlene Dumas. Museum images are rights-controlled and are linked, not reproduced here. The works named in the essay above are described, not shown.
